scope: Four consumers only; bighist3.5 remains frozen and byte-identical, no source review or source closure.

changes.note: For each overlap with nonconstant ring sequences, centre both vectors and divide their inner product by the product of their norms. Cauchy–Schwarz (ladr-6.14) bounds this Pearson correlation between −1 and 1; equality means proportional centred patterns. A high correlation alone does not establish a unique date: searching many lags, autocorrelation and shared trends still require the replication and filtering described above.

The random-event generator can be derived on its finite positive interval $[A,B]$. The fundamental theorem (pma-6.21) integrates $t^{-k}$: use $F(t)=(t^{1-k}-A^{1-k})/(B^{1-k}-A^{1-k})$ for $k\ne1$, and $F(t)=\ln(t/A)/\ln(B/A)$ for $k=1$. These strictly increasing CDFs map the endpoints to 0 and 1, so solving $F(t)=u$ for a uniform draw gives the displayed sampler. Separately, the fitted log–log line is the orthogonal projection of the vector $y_i=\log_{10}\Delta t_i$ onto the span of the constant vector and $x_i=\log_{10}t_i$ (ladr-6.61). With at least two distinct $x_i$, this gives the unique least-squares intercept and slope; it does not turn a selected milestone list into an unbiased historical test.

For the impact estimate, take the origin at the two-body centre of mass and write the relative position and velocity as $\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf v$. The centre-of-mass decomposition (mech-2.12), with $m_1\mathbf r_1+m_2\mathbf r_2=0$, reduces the orbital sum to $\mu\,\mathbf r\times\mathbf v$, where $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$. The angular-momentum lever-arm formula (mech-2.8) then gives its magnitude $\mu v b$ for the incoming relative trajectory. This is the orbital contribution; initial spins and the angular momentum carried by escaping material must be included in a full impact budget. The estimate alone does not establish the simulated disk composition.

The single-pole reconstruction uses the rigid-cap result geol-3.4: an orientation-preserving rigid displacement about Earth's fixed centre is one rotation about an Euler axis, and compositions are again such rotations. Thus a finite reconstruction needs a pole and an angle, while reversing its history uses inverse rotations in reverse order. This applies within the rigid-plate approximation; deforming boundaries and uncertainty in old poles are not removed by the rotation theorem.
